topic.title: API as architectural contract
topic.primary_concept: An API is a controlled interface and trust boundary between systems, not merely a URL that returns JSON.

lesson.problem_statement: Enterprises need systems owned by different teams or vendors to exchange data and trigger work without sharing databases, file shares, or direct server access.
lesson.concept_summary: Treat an API as (1) a contract of allowed requests/responses/errors, (2) a trust boundary for identity and authorization, and (3) an operational dependency where uptime, latency, versioning, and ownership concentrate. REST over HTTPS with JSON is a common shape; the architectural problem is the boundary.

sections.title: Architecture Concept
sections.body: What problem are we solving? Systems must talk across team and ownership lines without sharing internals. The API shrinks the attack and change surface to a deliberate interface.

sections.title: Connect to Something You Know
sections.body: Closest parallels: Windows service/RPC/WCF/SOAP endpoints; IIS behind an F5 VIP exposing only /api/...; SQL stored-proc layers so apps never touch base tables. Similarities: deliberate surface reduction. Limits: cloud APIs are often public/partner-facing; versioning is a product decision; auth is token/identity-based not NTLM/Kerberos to the box; backends may be ephemeral (Cloud Run), so host-centric thinking fails.

sections.title: Architecture Walkthrough
sections.body: Client/Partner → Internet → Akamai (edge/WAF) → DNS api.company.com → API Gateway/reverse proxy → Custom API (Cloud Run or IIS) → Downstream SQL/SaaS/Pub/Sub/other API. Inbound is typically synchronous HTTPS; downstream sync vs async is a separate design choice.

sections.title: Architect's View
sections.body: Approve designs only after ownership, AuthN vs AuthZ, network placement, TLS termination/re-encryption, dependency blast radius, failure modes, observability (correlation IDs), versioning strategy, and data classification in logs/responses are clear.

lesson.analogy_to_known: F5 VIP + IIS path + cert + auth policy ≈ API surface; stored-proc layer ≈ shrink data access surface.
lesson.analogy_limits: Public/partner exposure, productized versioning, OAuth/OIDC/JWT or service accounts instead of Kerberos-to-box, ephemeral compute instead of sticky hosts.
architect_view_bullets: Ownership of contract, on-call, and breaking changes
Public vs partner vs internal-only placement
Where TLS terminates and whether origin is re-encrypted
Every downstream call is SLA and blast radius
Consumer migration path when contract changes
What leaves the boundary in logs and responses
lesson.diagram_ascii:
Client / Partner / Browser SPA
        |
     Internet
        |
      Akamai  (edge / optional WAF)
        |
   Public DNS → api.company.com
        |
  API Gateway / reverse proxy
        |
   Custom API (e.g. Cloud Run or IIS)
        |
   Downstream: SQL / SaaS / Pub/Sub / another API

interactive_teach.prompt: Why call it a contract instead of an endpoint?
interactive_teach.reveal: Endpoint is location. Contract is behavior over time: schema, errors, auth, SLAs, and how breaking changes are managed.

interactive_teach.prompt: A valid JWT proves the caller is Service X, but X is not allowed to create LMS accounts. What failed?
interactive_teach.explain: AuthN established identity; AuthZ denied the action. Architects must design both.

interactive_teach.prompt: Name one way a Cloud Run–backed API breaks the classic IIS-behind-F5 mental model.
rubric_points: ephemeral instances / no sticky host assumption
scaling and cold start change failure modes
public ingress patterns differ from corp LAN VIP

scenario.prompt: An internal HR web app (on-prem, IIS behind F5) must create accounts in a SaaS LMS when a new hire is approved. The LMS exposes a REST API on the public internet. Security will not allow the IIS servers to have unrestricted outbound internet. The LMS team wants a stable enterprise endpoint they can allowlist and audit, not 40 app servers calling them directly.
questions: What components would you put between the HR app and the LMS API, and why?
Where would you terminate TLS, and would you re-encrypt?
How should the HR app authenticate to your side, vs how your side authenticates to the LMS?
What fails if the LMS is down for 30 minutes — and what should the architecture do about that?
scenario.ui_hint: Collect free-text design answer; do not show a model solution until Greg critiques or learner requests reveal.

knowledge_check.question: Why might we put an API gateway in front of a Cloud Run (or IIS) service instead of exposing it directly?
rubric_points: central auth, rate limits, WAF integration
stable public contract vs backend churn
observability and policy enforcement choke point

knowledge_check.question: A partner can reach api.company.com and TLS succeeds, but every call returns 401. Which layer is most likely healthy vs failing?
rubric_points: AuthN failing (missing/invalid token or wrong audience)

knowledge_check.question: Security blocks unrestricted outbound internet from IIS. How does that constraint change where the LMS integration should live?
rubric_points: egress via controlled proxy/API tier or integration service
stable SNAT/egress IP for vendor allowlist
not 40 app servers each with open egress

knowledge_check.question: If the LMS is unavailable for 30 minutes, is a synchronous create-account call from the HR approval click good architecture? Why or why not?
rubric_points: user-facing sync couples HR UX to SaaS uptime
prefer queue/async with retry/DLQ for durable business events
still need status/visibility for ops and HR

one_thing_to_remember: Design the API as a trust boundary and owned contract first; the URL and JSON schema are implementation details of that boundary.
